problem: Interactive Navigation means reaching a goal that requires physically interacting with the environment along the way, e.g. opening a door with a mobile manipulator. It is long-horizon, has sparse reward, and is heterogeneous: the task mixes pure navigation, pure manipulation and combined phases. Flat RL gets stuck in local optima. Existing HRL methods (HIRO, HAC) only set subgoals in the same space as the final goal and always use the whole embodiment.
motivation: Robots in human environments must open doors or push obstacles to navigate, which requires a mobile base with an arm. Using the whole embodiment in every phase wastes energy and raises collision risk. The task naturally splits into phases whose goals live in different spaces (base location vs. end-effector pose), which fits a hierarchy where the high level picks both the phase type and the subgoal.
key_idea: A two-level PPO hierarchy in which the high-level policy outputs two things every T steps: (1) a relative subgoal on mutable observation dimensions (the end-effector position), and (2) a discrete embodiment selector (base-only / arm-only / base+arm) that masks both the low-level action and the subgoal dimensions used for intrinsic reward.
insight: Temporally extended commitment to subgoals gives deeper exploration than flat PPO. Flat PPO converges quickly to a local reward maximum (driving toward the wall between rooms), while HRL4IN eventually solves the door-opening task. HAC fails because its hindsight goals cluster near the start position and do not match the final-goal distribution. The Gibson ablation (Table 1) shows that removing the embodiment selector keeps success similar (0.912 vs 0.963) but energy-saving drops to 0.0. Removing r_energy reduces energy-saving to 0.235. Removing r_progress or r_collision gives 0.0 success, so the method depends heavily on shaped rewards. The learned selector is interpretable: base-only nearly everywhere, base+arm only in front of the door to grasp the handle. The policy then switches back to base-only and opens the door by moving the base while holding the handle.
method: High-level policy: a PPO policy with CNN+MLP features and a GRU. Conditioned on the final goal, it acts every T low-level steps (T=4 in ToyEnv, T=50 = 5 s in Gibson), or earlier if the subgoal is reached. It outputs a continuous relative subgoal g on mutable observation dims (end-effector xyz in Gibson; agent x, y, yaw and door state in ToyEnv) plus a discrete embodiment selector. The two action losses are summed.

Embodiment selector → masks: the selector yields an action mask that zeroes the velocities of unused joints (e.g. all arm joints for base-only). It also yields a subgoal mask that picks which subgoal dims count for intrinsic reward (z is masked out for base-only, giving a 2D xy subgoal).

Low-level policy: a PPO GRU policy acting every step. It is conditioned on observation, the relative subgoal (re-expressed each step as x_t' + g − x_t), and both masks. It outputs joint velocities for 2 wheels + 5 arm joints, which are then masked.
Intrinsic reward: r_LL = D_t − D_{t+1}, where D is the masked Euclidean distance to the absolute subgoal (scaled ×30). A subgoal counts as reached if D < 0.05 m (continuous) or D = 0 (discrete).

High-level reward: the sum of extrinsic environment rewards over the subgoal execution window. The Gibson extrinsic reward is a weighted sum of success (30), phase-wise progress (2), energy (−0.001 per actuated base/arm) and collision (−0.01).

Training: both levels are trained jointly on-policy with PPO. The high level is frozen for the first 500 updates. High-level LR is 1e-5, low-level LR 1e-4, with 256 rollout steps and GAE. On-policy training is chosen to reduce non-stationarity from the changing low-level policy.

Environments: a new 2D grid-world 'Interactive ToyEnv' (11×11, door needs 5 slide-up actions), and 'Interactive Gibson Environment', which extends Gibson with simulated articulated doors. It uses a JackRabbot robot (Segway base + Kinova arm) and a grasp primitive that attaches a ball joint when the end-effector is within 0.1 m of the handle.

setting.backbone: Two CNN+MLP+GRU (hidden 512) policies (high-level and low-level), trained from scratch with PPO
setting.training_data: On-policy RL in a single fixed layout. Interactive Gibson Env: ~6 m × 9 m two-room layout with one door, fixed start with random orientation, ~50M env steps, 5 seeds. Interactive ToyEnv: 11×11 grid with two rooms and a door, 7 seeds. No external data.
setting.observation: Gibson: 64×64 depth map (clipped at 5 m) + proprioception (end-effector xyz, base pose/velocities, roll/pitch/yaw, joint positions/velocities/torques, collision and grasp flags) + door angle/location + goal location. ToyEnv: 4-channel top-down global map + agent pose + door state + goal.
setting.action_space: Gibson: continuous joint velocities for 2 wheels + 5 arm joints (7 DoF), with an automatic grasp primitive. ToyEnv: discrete turn-left/turn-right/go-forward/no-op + slide-up/slide-down/no-op.
setting.simulator: Interactive Gibson Environment (Gibson extension with physics / articulated doors) and a 2D grid-world (Interactive ToyEnv)
setting.privileged: Door angle and location, goal position and robot/end-effector poses come directly from the simulator state; ToyEnv provides a full top-down global map. A scripted grasp primitive attaches to the door handle when the end-effector is within 0.1 m. Training and evaluation use the same single layout.

The number of evaluation episodes behind Table 1 is not stated.
results: In the Interactive Gibson door-opening task, HRL4IN reaches 0.963 success, 64.3 reward and 0.453 energy-saving (Table 1). Flat PPO gets stuck in a local maximum (driving toward the wall between the rooms) and HAC fails completely; per the training curves, neither baseline solves the task. In the grid-world ToyEnv, HRL4IN solves the task in 5/7 seeds vs 3/7 for flat PPO. Its best seed reaches 100% success in 19.2 steps on average vs a 14-step optimum (<1.5× optimal), though training is less stable and initially less sample-efficient.
limitations: Evaluated only in one fixed hand-built layout (single door, fixed start location), with no generalization to unseen scenes and no real-robot transfer (stated as future work).
Relies on privileged simulator state (door angle/location, goal position) and a scripted grasp primitive that attaches to the handle within 0.1 m, simplifying contact-rich manipulation.
Depends heavily on reward shaping: without r_progress or r_collision success drops to 0. Joint HL/LL training is less stable and initially less sample-efficient than flat PPO.
builds_on: HIRO (Nachum et al. 2018, data-efficient HRL with relative subgoals)
